Board Important – Karnataka 2nd PUC Question Bank

Biotechnology and its Applications tests real-world uses of genetic engineering – mechanism-based flowchart questions (Bt toxin, RNAi, gene therapy) are asked almost every year, and it overlaps heavily with NEET.
~9–11 marksApplication-based chapter, strongly favoured for 5-mark mechanism/flowchart questions
4 × 5 MBt cotton/Bt toxin mechanism, RNAi silencing pathway, recombinant insulin (humulin) production, ADA deficiency gene therapy
4 × 3 MTransgenic animals & their uses, molecular diagnosis (PCR/ELISA), GEAC role, biopiracy & ethical issues
4 × 2 MGolden rice, Cry genes, gene therapy definition, GM & Bt definitions

⭐⭐⭐ Top priority – almost always asked (5 marks)

  • Bt cotton & mechanism of Bt toxin action (5 M) – Bacillus thuringiensis Cry proteins exist as inactive protoxins; once ingested by an insect (e.g. bollworm), the alkaline gut solubilises the protein → activated toxin binds midgut epithelial receptors → creates pores → cell lysis → insect death. The specific cry gene (e.g. cryIAc, cryIIAb) is introduced into the cotton genome, making the plant insect-resistant.
  • RNA interference (RNAi) – mechanism (5 M) – used naturally by some viruses/transposons; introduced dsRNA is recognised and cut by the enzyme Dicer into siRNAs → siRNA binds a complementary specific mRNA → causes its silencing/degradation. Used commercially in tobacco to make nematode-resistant plants by triggering RNAi in the parasite Meloidogyne incognitae.
  • Production of recombinant human insulin (5 M) – Eli Lilly prepared 2 DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin, introduced them into plasmids of E. coli, produced the chains separately, then extracted and combined them by creating disulfide bonds to form mature (biologically active) human insulin – unlike bovine/porcine insulin, this doesn't trigger an immune reaction.
  • Gene therapy for Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency (5 M) – lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture, a functional ADA cDNA is introduced into these lymphocytes using a retroviral vector, and the cells are reintroduced into the patient's body; bone-marrow cells containing the ADA gene producing stem cells provide a more permanent cure.

⭐⭐ High priority – frequently asked (3 marks)

  • Transgenic animals & their uses (3 M) – animals with a manipulated genome, used to study how genes are regulated, to test disease models (e.g. cancer, cystic fibrosis), for biological product testing (e.g. transgenic mice carrying human genes for testing vaccine safety), and for producing biological products (proteins in milk, e.g. alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema treatment).
  • Molecular diagnosis by PCR & ELISA (3 M) – PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies a pathogen's nucleic acid to detectable levels even at very low concentrations for early diagnosis (e.g. HIV); ELISA is based on the antigen-antibody interaction principle, detecting the presence of infection by testing for antigens or antibodies.
  • Role of GEAC & biosafety issues (3 M) – the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee is the statutory body under India's Ministry of Environment and Forests responsible for deciding the validity/safety of GM research and the release of GM organisms/products for public use.
  • Biopiracy & the need for its prevention (3 M) – the unauthorised, uncompensated use of biological resources or traditional knowledge by companies/organisations without approval from the country and its people (e.g. turmeric/basmati patent disputes); India has amended its Patent Act to prevent this.
  • Golden Rice (3 M) – a genetically modified rice variety with vitamin A (beta-carotene) fortified into the endosperm, developed to address vitamin A deficiency – a good example of GM applications for nutritional improvement.

⭐ Two-mark favourites – learn as clean pairs

  • GM (Genetically Modified) organism vs Bt crop (specific GM organism carrying a Bacillus thuringiensis toxin gene).
  • Somatic gene therapy (corrects cells of the individual only, effect not inherited) vs germline gene therapy (would be inherited, currently not practised/permitted).
  • Cry proteins cryIAc & cryIIAb (control cotton bollworms) vs cryIAb (controls corn borer).
  • PCR (amplifies DNA for detection) vs ELISA (detects antigen-antibody reaction).
  • GEAC (approves/regulates GM research & products in India) vs biopiracy (unauthorised commercial use of bioresources/traditional knowledge).
Answer-writing tip: for every mechanism question (Bt toxin, RNAi, insulin production, gene therapy), write the answer as a numbered, arrow-linked sequence of steps rather than a paragraph – examiners award marks for each correctly sequenced step.
Never lose these marks: always spell out full forms correctly on first use – GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee), ADA (Adenosine Deaminase), PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction), RNAi (RNA interference) – and never confuse somatic with germline gene therapy.

Important Diagrams

📖 Every high-yield figure in this chapter, ranked by board-exam priority with its typical mark weightage, the exact labels you must show, and a direct link to the matching page of the official NCERT PDF — so you always know which diagrams matter most and where to see them.

GM Crops & RNAi

Fig 10.1 — Mechanism of Bt Toxin Action 5 M ★★★ Top Priority
Draw as a flowchart: inactive Cry protoxin ingested → alkaline gut activates toxin → toxin binds midgut epithelial receptors → pore formation → cell lysis → insect death. Label the cry gene inserted into the cotton plant.
View page 178 in NCERT PDF →
Fig 10.2 — RNAi Silencing Pathway in Nematode-Resistant Tobacco 5 M ★★★ Top Priority
Show sense & anti-sense RNA introduced into the tobacco host cell → form dsRNA → Dicer enzyme cuts into siRNA → siRNA binds and silences the nematode's specific mRNA → nematode cannot survive in the transgenic host, preventing infestation.
View page 180 in NCERT PDF →

Medical Biotechnology

Fig 10.3 — Production of Recombinant Insulin (Humulin) 5 M ★★★ Top Priority
Show two separate E. coli plasmid cultures, one producing insulin chain A and the other chain B → both chains extracted → combined by forming disulfide (–S–S–) bonds → mature, biologically-active human insulin (Humulin).
View page 182 in NCERT PDF →
Fig 10.4 — Gene Therapy Procedure for ADA Deficiency 5 M ★★★ Top Priority
Show lymphocytes withdrawn from the patient's blood → grown in culture → functional ADA cDNA introduced via a retroviral vector → genetically corrected cells reintroduced into the patient's body, alongside bone-marrow stem cells for a more permanent cure.
View page 182 in NCERT PDF →
